Vivaraṇaprameyasaṅgraha
------------------------------------------
The Advaita Vedānta has been expounded by शङ्कर (A.

-820) in his bhāṣya or commentary on the Brahma-sūtras of बादरायण, especially in the first four sūtras. पद्मपाद (9th century A. D.), a direct disciple of शङ्कर, has written a commentary on it called Pañca-pādikā. This was further commented upon by प्रकाशात्मन् (A.
), which he named as Pañcapādikā Vivaraṇa, starting the Vivaraṇa school of Advaita as different from the भामती school of वाचस्पति (A.

).
The Vivaraṇaprameyasaṅgraha attri-buted to विद्यारण्य (14th century A. D.) is a scholarly polemical work in prose in nine varṇakas or chapters. It tries to give a detailed exposition of the various basic concepts of Advaita, especially अविद्या (nescience), according to the Vivaraṇa school.
The work is sometimes attributed to Bhāratītīrtha.
See also ADVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA.

vivekakhyāti
(‘knowledge born out of विवेक or discrimination’)
------------------------------------------
See SĀṄKHYA-DARŚANA.

Vivekacūḍāmaṇi
(‘crestjewel of discrimination’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the finest prakaraṇagranthas or elementary treatises of Advaita Vedānta by शङ्कर (A.

-820). It is in verses of various metres, the total number being 579. There is a balanced combination of philosophical acumen and literary grace in this work.
It has only two commentaries: the older one by Keśavācāryasvāmin of Munimaṇḍala; the other by Candraśekhara-भारती (A.

-1954), a former pontiff of the Śāradāpīṭha of Śṛṅgerī.
A very brief account of its contents may now be set forth here: importance of attaining मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्; means of attaining it; place of भक्ति or devotion in the path of लिबेरतिओन्; importance of self-effort; लिबेरतिओन् can be attained only by the knowledge of the identity of jīvātman (the individual सोउल्) and पर-mātman (the Supreme सोउल्); māyā and its two powers; nature of the आत्मन्; means of destroying the bondage of सṁसार or transmigratory existence; nature of ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute; explanation of the mahāvākya tat-tvam-asi; fruit of ātma-ज्ञान or realisation of the आत्मन्, the Self; characteristics of the jīvanmukta, the liberated सोउल्; on प्रारब्धकर्म (karma that has started giving its results); conclusion of the treatise.
See also ŚAṄKARA.

viveka
(‘discrimination’)
------------------------------------------
This is the first of the four disciplines mentioned under साधनचतुष्टय. It means discrimination that helps an aspirant to distinguish the real from the unreal, the eternal from the non-eternal. For instance, the body is non-eternal (and hence unreal in essence) whereas the आत्मन् (the सोउल्) is eternal and hence real.

vivartavāda
(‘the doctrine of apparent transformation’)
------------------------------------------
The basic cause of an erroneous perception, as that of a snake in rope, is called अज्ञान or अविद्या. It has two powers: āvaraṇaśakti (veiling power) and vikṣepaśakti (transforming power). It veils the real nature of the rope and apparently transforms it into a snake. This apparently transformed object is called a ‘vivarta’ of the original and the theory that propounds it is known as विवर्तवाद.
See also KHYĀTI.

Vivekānanda, Svāmi
------------------------------------------
1. The Descent
An overwhelming number of human beings are just products of history. But, once in a while, the world throws up from its bosom, such extraordinary geniuses who create history. Nay, they are history, if we redefine history as ‘his story’. It is the story of such men—the salt of the earth—who shape the destinies of millions of human beings for millenniums, that is real history!
Rāmas and Kṛṣṇas of the most ancient period, Buddhas and Christs of the remote past, were such epoch-making personalities. To this list should be added रामकृष्ण and Vivekānanda of the recent past, the movement in whose names is gaining greater and greater momentum.
As per one of the profound mystical visions of रामकृष्ण, Vivekānanda was one of the Seven Great Sages who descended to this earth out of his own free-will, to help mankind to rediscover its inherent divinity.
The earthly advent of Narendranāth Datta—that was his premonastic name—took place on the 12th January 1863 at Calcutta (now Kolkata). His ड़थेर् Viśva-nātha Datta was an attorney. भुवनेश्वरी देवी, his मोथेर्, was a highly cultured and pious lady.
Under their loving care, Narendra grew up into a fine boy.
2. Child Prodigy
Even in his early boyhood, Narendra exhibited many extraordinary traits and talents indicating his future greatness. Exceptionally brilliant intelligence, a prodigious memory, a generous heart that felt for the poor and the downtrodden, absolute fearlessness, utter contempt for superstitious beliefs and a regal bearing were conspicuous in him by their compelling presence.
Though he would often neglect attending the school regularly due to his tremendous attraction for manly sports and voracious reading habits, he would invariably pass the examinations creditably.
By the time he reached the college for higher studies, he had already mastered many a difficult text of Western philosophy and लोगिच्.
3. The Restless Search
Delving into deep meditation—even from early boyhood days—was as natural to him as a fish swimming in deep waters.
Though meditation had brought him some inner peace, the intellectual restlessness brought about by an innate desire to know God—if He really existed—and the various metaphysical treatises (bordering on agnosticism or even अथेइस्म्) he had thoroughly gone through, increased to such an extent that he started visiting any and every person considered as or appearing to be a holy man or a man of God. Neither anyone of them, nor even the well-known leaders of the Brahma Samāj, could whet his spiritual appetite by giving a direct and unambiguous, positive, answer.
Vivekānanda4. The Search Ends
Rāmakṛṣṇa (A.

-1886)—more well-known as the Paramahaṁsa—had already become a household name in Calcutta. Though Narendra had heard about him (and had also seen him once in the होउसे of a devotee at Calcutta), he had not cared to go and meet him, thinking that he was an unlettered rustic and hence it was not worth seeing him. However, persuaded by Rāmacandra Datta (A.

-1899), a close relative (of Narendra) as also a disciple of रामकृष्ण, he decided to go to Dakṣiṇeśvar and meet the saint.
This first encounter, wherein Narendra got a direct answer in the affir-mative, for his (eternal) direct question—‘Sir! Have you seen God?’—not only thrilled him but also confused him. It confused him because of the great Master रामकृष्ण’s strange behaviour of addressing him as नारायण (Lord विष्णु), shedding tears profusely and talking to him as if he had known him intimately for ages!
Whereas the Master was talking from the standpoint of his high mystical experience, Narendra was too dumbfounded to understand it.
Thus the search for a true godman ended for

Narendra.
5

. The Struggle Begins
It is one thing to know that the godman has truly realised God and entirely another thing to be trained by him to get the same experience oneself !
The next five years were a period of intense training by the great गुरु, of the great disciple.
While the former wanted to cast the latter in a supermould, to carry on and continue his work even after he was gone, the latter fought every inch of his way before accepting it, unless duly convinced.
The period of apprenticeship often appeared more like a battle between equals than a training session. On one side was a well-educated strong young man, equipped with a razor-sharp intellect, bolstered by a deep knowledge of Western philosophy, science and लोगिच्. On the other side was an uneducated ब्राह्मण priest from a backward village of the 19th century Bengal, whose one and only asset was the constant companionship of Kālī, the Divine मोथेर्, whose very existence was doubted, and the image detested, by the likes of Narendra.
Ultimately it was रामकृष्ण that triumphed in the war though he seemed to lose some battles, the battles of wits. In such cases, what he could not achieve through लोगिच्, he successfully did by magic, by his magic touch, imparting instant experience of the Divine.
Domestic tragedies like the sudden demise of his ड़थेर् and the consequent penury of the family as also the desertion by his (so-called) friends, made Narendra surrender himself totally at the feet of his गुरु, whose love and faith had, all along, remained absolutely unshaken.
During this period, a direct, most wondrous, experience of मोथेर् Kālī, vouchsafed by the grace of the गुरु, put an end to all the doubts and vacillations of the disciple. His चोन्वेर्सिओन् or transformation was now complete.
6. ‘Keep the Flock Together’
During रामकृष्ण’s stay at the temple garden of Dakṣiṇeśvar, the Brāhmo Movement (started originally by राजा राम्मोहन् रोय्) (A.
-1833) was at its zenith. It is a strange irony that an important leader of this protestant movement against traditional or orthodox Hinduism—Keśab चन्द्र Sen (A.

-1884)—became instrumental in publicising the greatness of the परमहṁस of Dakṣiṇeśvar, thereby bringing the cream of ‘young Bengal’ (educated youth of Bengal) in great numbers to one who was the very antithesis of all for which the Brāhmo Movement stood!
Quite a few of these young men became his ardent disciples, deeply interested in totally dedicating themselves to spiritual pursuits, by adopting the monastic life.
Rāmakṛṣṇa trained them so adroitly that each one of them got not only general guidance but also the teachings parti-cularly suited to him.
When he fell ill due to cancer of the throat in the middle of A.

and later was completely bedridden, he was moved to a होउसे, first in Śyāmpukūr (Shyamapukur) and later, to a spacious bungalow with an extensive garden in Kāśīpūr (Cossipore).
It was here, that the great Master bound his young disciples—who were serving him day and night by turns—into a well-knit body of future monastics, with Narendra as their undisputed leader.
After imparting detailed instructions to the leader as to the continuation of his work and commanding him to ‘keep the flock together,’ the great Master ascended to his heavenly abode on the 16th August 1886, the day he himself had chosen to depart from this world.
7. The Broken होउसे and the Unbroken Spirit
As ordained by his Master, Narendra arranged to rent a house—a broken and highly dilapidated one—at Barānagar (in Calcutta) for the stay of all the young men chosen by him for the monastic life. This was the first monastery of the Ramakrishna Order. In fact,—probably in January 1886—the Master had distributed with his own hands, ochre robes to twelve of these young men. They now formed the nucleus of the Ramakrishna Order of मोन्क्स्.
Under the leadership of Narendra, all of them formally embraced monastic life with proper vows and new monastic names. Narendra is supposed to have adopted the new name Vividiṣānanda though he would sometimes change it to Saccidānanda during his itinerant days so as not to be found out by his brother disciples. However, he later on assumed the name Vivekānanda permanently.
Though these young मोन्क्स् had to live in a god-forsaken place infested with poisonous reptiles outside and a ramshackle roof on their heads, their spirit was unbroken and the determination to realise the goal of their life, adamantine.
Spurred by the age-old urge of saṁnyāsins to lead a wandering life, depending entirely on God, the young recluses left the monastery one by one. Only Śaśi (Rāmakṛṣṇānanda) stayed put, to take care of the relics of his Master housed in this monastery and care for the other brothers who stayed back.
Vivekānanda was no exception to this ‘mad’ urge. After a few short sojourns here and there, he left the Math as an itinerant monk, this time to closely observe and study India in all her aspects.
8. Unknown Expedition for a Known Destination
Apparently, Vivekānanda’s expedition was into the unknown or the little-known facts of India—its land, its people, its religion and culture, its hopes and aspirations, its glories and mistakes, its miseries and sufferings; in short, India in its totality, at first-hand.
This was absolutely necessary for him to know—even as a doctor had to know all about his patient before prescribing his remedies—since he had been specially ordained by his Master to work vigorously for the uplift of his motherland.
Thus it was that, though his expedition was into the unknown, his destination or the final goal was clearly known.
Vivekānanda’s experiences as an itinerant monk were as diverse as they were direct too. He could see India’s people and their life at close quarters—now in the palaces of the kings or the mansions of the rich, and, the next day sleeping in the cottages of the poor who could hardly manage a square meal per day, or with their animals in the sheds. Vivekānanda could realise how poverty, इग्नोरन्चे and squalour were everywhere, and how the common masses who had been oppressed and exploited for ages, had become next-door neighbours to brutes.
However, to his pleasant surprise, he discovered that the true spirit of religion (as he called it) was still very much present in the Indian blood. He realised that religion was the backbone of India and that she could rise (or had to be raised) only through that.
After visiting the Himālayan shrines, travelling through the fertile Indo-Gangetic plains, meandering through the Rājasthān deserts in scorching sun and the Deccan plateau, he finally landed in the कन्याकुमारी temple-town (known as चपे चोमोरिन् then).
Offering his obeisance first in the shrine he went to the sea-shore where the Indian Ocean absorbs into its bosom, the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. Seeing two rocks in the ocean at a short distance and unable to withstand the temptation of their call as it were, he swam to the bigger one and sat there in a restful state, gradually souring into deep meditation.
9. Future Revealed
By now he had seen enough of India at first-hand. He had intuited its glorious past. He had observed its present degradation. He had discovered its causes and also devised the solutions. The only thing that had to be done now was their implementation.
Earlier, during his travels through Gujarat and Madras City (now Chennai), some friends and devotees had suggested, nay, had even pressurised him, that he should go to America and attend the Parliament of Religions. Though he was receptive to the idea, he was not sure whether it had his Master’s approval. His own vision of रामकृष्ण walking over the sea towards the west and beckoning him to follow, as also a similar one vouchsafed to Śrī Sāradādevī (A.

-1920), the divine consort of the Master, removed all doubts from his मिन्द्.
His plan of action was now clear and vivid in his मिन्द्. He would go to America, earn money by the power of his brains, return to India and build an organisation of मोन्क्स् to serve the poor and the downtrodden. Through the twin ideals of renunciation and service to mankind, he would attempt to raise India not only to its past glory but even beyond that!
Spurred and enthused by this vision, and with an unshakable faith in his गुरु, he returned to Madras. After visiting Khetri in Rajasthan whose king was his disciple, he set sail for America from Bombay (now Mumbai) on the 31st May 1893.
His disciples at Madras as also the Mahārājā of Khetri provided him with the necessary money and baggage.
Travelling via Ceylon (now Sri Lanka), China and Japan, he finally reached Chicago on the 30th July, where the Parliament of Religions was scheduled to be held.
However, he was shocked to learn that the Parliament was still three months away.
With help coming from the most unexpected quarters, he shifted to Boston—since it was less expensive—and returned to Chicago on time to attend the Parliament as an official delegate of हिन्दुइस्म् from

India.
10

. The East Storms the West
The Parliament of Religions was held from the 11th to the 27th of September 1893 in the Hall of Columbus, as a part of the World’s Columbian Exposition.
On the inaugural day, Vivekānanda, who had been seated on the vast dais along with a host of delegates from different parts of the world, representing various religions, was a little awed at the great crowd and the august occasion.
However, when he rose to speak, almost towards the end of the day, remembering मोथेर् सरस्वती, the goddess of learning, he was a totally transfigured person. The very first words he uttered, a short address of just five words—‘Sisters and Brothers of America!’ electrified the audience, a huge mass of humanity, into a thunderous clapping session lasting for over two minutes!
Obviously, the East had stormed the citadel of the West in a matter of a few seconds!
It was a short talk, but scintillating with the spirit of universality, perfectly in tune with the ethos of the Parliament. It stressed the universal spiritual truth that all paths, whether crooked or straight, would ultimately lead to the same Godhead.
In an instant, the simple monk with a begging bowl, had become the man of the hour, the uncrowned king of countless admirers.
11. Hectic Tours to Transmit Tranquillity
The Master had wanted him to become like a huge banyan tree giving shelter to thousands in its protective shade, rather than be a recluse interested only in his own लिबेरतिओन्. The time for it had arrived now.
During the period September 1893 to August 1895, Vivekānanda had a hectic time visiting places, giving lectures and parlour talks, granting personal interviews, taking classes for earnest students of Vedānta, addressing the gathering at well-known universities as also exchange ideas with the best brains of America like Prof. William James (A.
-1910), Prof. J. H. Wright, Robert Ingersoll (A.

-1899) and others.
It was during this time (June 1895) that he delivered his now famous Inspired Talks to a small but serious group of twelve disciples at Miss Dutcher’s cottage in the Thousand Island Park.
As a result of his tireless efforts through such teaching and preaching, the Americans were able to understand and appreciate हिन्दुइस्म् better, thereby abandoning many a misconception, dispelled by his forceful expositions.
His unexpected presence and the spectacular success in America often led to persecution and even character assassination, by certain Christian zealots as well as some of his own jealous countrymen. However, the vigorous defence put up by his western disciples silenced them.
He visited England also during the period September 1895 up to April 1896. Here too his success was remarkable. And, what is more, he made a few excellent disciples like Mr. and Mrs. Sevier, J. J. Goodwin (A.
-1898) and Miss Margaret Noble (Sister Niveditā) (A.

-1911).
He also had the opportunity of meeting Prof. Max Muller (at Oxford in England) (A.
-1900) and Prof. Deussen (at Kiel in Germany) (A.

-1919).
12. Back to the Motherland
After laying a firm foundation for his work in America and England, and placing his brother disciples, Svāmis Sāradānanda (A.
-1927) and Abhedānanda (A.

-1939) in charge of the work, Vivekānanda returned to India, along with Mr. and Mrs. Sevier as also J. J. Goodwin, via Ceylon. He arrived at Colombo on the 15th January 1897 to a tumultous welcome by a sea of humanity.
Then, travelling through the various cities and towns of the Madras Presidency (now Tamil Nadu) he arrived in Madras.
Here he delivered about six lectures to mammoth audiences—which the city had never witnessed earlier—each scintillating with the power and the pride of Indian nationalism.
After acceding to the request of the local devotees and admirers to start a centre of his work at Madras, he sailed to Calcutta, his hometown, reaching there on the 19th February 1897.
The city of Calcutta gave a fitting reception to the Son of the Soil.
During his long absence, the Math had been shifted from Barānagar to Alambazar in 1892 and later, to the garden होउसे of Nīlāmbar Mukherjī in 1897.
13. Sleeping Giant Awakened
Now began another hectic period in Vivekānanda’s life.
His talks in America were aimed at vigorously propagating true हिन्दुइस्म् through Vedānta, and removing all the misconceptions about it, deliberately spread by the mischievous and bigoted propaganda of the Christian missionaries.
India however, needed an entirely different approach and treatment.
So, he now started on another lecture expedition—which he had begun at Colombo itself—singularly aimed at rousing the Indian nation by demolishing its superstitions—the accretions over several centuries—total lack of self-confidence and the mania of blindly imitating the West. He reminded his audiences of their past glory and greatness, castigated them for their ‘kitchen and the cooking-pot religion’ of exclusivity, their oppression of the lower castes and groups as also keeping their women in इग्नोरन्चे by denying them एदुचतिओन्.
These lectures, now famous as the Lectures from Colombo to Almora are the modern Veda he has bequeathed to Modern India.
The result was a galvanisation of the Indian morale and a great fillip to the movement for political freedom, whose leaders derived great inspiration from him.
14. Mission Accomplished
For several years, Vivekānanda had been cherishing a great desire in his heart, an intense yearning, to establish the urn containing the relics of his great Master and mentor, in a permanent place and build a monastery round it. This monastery, wherein will live the Master’s disciples and their disciples, thus forming a new monastic tradition and Order, will give a practical shape to his command to rejuvenate हिन्दुइस्म् as also rebuild the motherland.
When he sent Svāmi Rāmakṛṣṇā-नन्द (A.

-1911) to Madras, to start a Math there to continue his work, he had already made a beginning in this direction.
On the 1st May 1897, he called a meeting of all the monastic and lay disciples of the great Master रामकृष्ण in the होउसे of Balarām Bose (A.

-1890) and formed the organisation ‘Ramakrishna Mission Association’.
Later, he purchased a plot of land on the western bank of the river गङ्गा and built a monastery with a shrine there.
He himself carried the urn containing the relics of रामकृष्ण, established it there and performed the consecration ceremony with all the attendant rituals. This was on the 9th December 1898.
This Math has now become well-known as the Belur Math and houses the Headquarters of the Ramakrishna Order.
Having thus accomplished a great mission he had cherished for long, he could now rest in peace.
Meanwhile, a good number of young men had joined the monastic order established by him. His own brother disciples—the monastic disciples of Rāmakṛṣṇa—too were living there. Hence Vivekānanda turned his attention now to the training of these young novices, with their help.
15. Pilgrimages and Tours
Vivekānanda found some time to go on a few pilgrimages, the notable places being Amarnāth and Kṣīrbhavānī, both in Kashmir.
In both the places he observed diligently all the ceremonials and rituals prescribed for ordinary pilgrims as if to set an example to them.
He seems to have had some profound spiritual experiences during these pilgrimages.
He now decided to go to the West a second time, more to see how the work there was progressing. Accompanied by Svāmi Turīyānanda (A.

-1922) and Sister Niveditā, he first visited England for two weeks (in July 1899) and later went to America in August. He was happy to see how Svāmi Abhedānanda had established the Vedānta work on a firm foundation. He left Svāmi Turīyānanda on the west-coast at San Antone Valley, to establish a Retreat Centre (now known as the Śānti आश्रम). After attending the Parliament of History of Religions in Paris and spending about three months there he returned to Calcutta on the 9th December 1900.
16. The Ascent
Rāmakṛṣṇa had predicted two things about his ‘Naren’ (Vivekānanda): That he would not reach his 40th year of his life; and that, the moment he discovered who he was, he would voluntarily cast off the physical body.
A few days before his passing away, he confided to one of his brother-disciples, in answer to a question inadvertently put to him, that he now knew who he was.
Three days before his final departure from this world, he instructed Svāmi Premānanda where to cremate his body!
He had even fixed the date as it were, after scrutinising the Beṅgālī almanac, a week earlier.
On the last day of his life—the 4th of July 1902—he rose from his bed very early, meditated in the shrine room (after closing all the doors and the windows) for an unusually long time, took a class on Sanskrit grammar for the brahmacārins (tyros under training) for three hours, had a long stroll in the evening and then retired to his room at the time of vesper service in the shrine.
After meditating for some time he lay down on the bed, spread on the floor and quietly breathed his last at 9 P.M.
It was noticed that the eyes were bloodshot and a little blood had oozed through the nostrils and the mouth, indicating the departure of life through the ब्रह्मरन्ध्र (the aperture in the crown of the head).
The body was cremated at the very spot he had indicated. A magnificent memorial temple stands on that spot now, beckoning all to come to him and be inspired.
17. Character and Personality
A sound मिन्द् in a sound body, fully reflecting a spirit that is always sound—this is how Vivekānanda’s person and personality can be described.
Physically, he was well-built and handsome. Gymnastics, games, swimming and wrestling were his favourite pastimes during early youth.
Intellectually, he was a giant. Photo-graphic memory and a razor-sharp intellect helped him to master any subject in no time. By just glancing through a book he could not only reveal its contents but also often quote it verbatim.
Oratory was his special and most natural gift. When he spoke, tremendous power would appear to be emanating from him, transporting his audience to a plane where they would be listening to a voice from the void as it were.
He was an expert musician too. Endowed with a rich and melodious voice, cultured by years of training in classical मुसिच्, his singing, especially of devotional songs and hymns, could enthrall even the most prosaic hearts. He was also good at playing many a musical instrument.
Though most of his literary works are records of his inspiring—and extempore—talks, he has left us a few written compositions in Sanskrit, Beṅgālī and English, like hymns, poems and thoughtful essays. It is now acknowledged that he was a pioneer in the च्रेअतिओन् of a new style of Beṅgālī prose.
His great poem—The Song of the Saṁnyāsin—reverberating with the fiery feeling of a monk’s inner stuff and psyche, is a masterpiece of English literature soaked in the Eastern spirit.
His power of meditation was astounding. (Even from the childhood days, he could sit still in meditation like a statue, for a long time.) रामकृष्ण had declared that he was a dhyānasiddha, a sage perfected in meditation and had descended to the earth from the region of the सप्तर्षिस्, the Seven Sages of Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य्.
In spite of the majestic external appearance, striking awe in the minds of the onlookers, he possessed a heart that was simple like that of a child and yet infinitely tender towards the sufferings of others.
In short, he personified in himself the perfect man—with शङ्कर’s intellect and the बुद्ध’s heart—that he wanted everyone to become, in life.
18. The Philosophy of Vivekānanda
Vivekānanda has given his philo-sophy of life succinctly in two places. At the beginning of his remarkable treatise Rājayoga he has given the following aphoristic maxims which can be called the Catussūtrī (Four Aphorisms) of नेओ-वेदान्त:
Each सोउल् is potentially Divine.
The goal is to manifest this Divine within by controlling Nature, external and internal.
Do this either by work, or worship, or psychic control, or by philosophy, by one, or more, or all of these—and be free!
This is the whole of religion. Doctrines or dogmas, or rituals, or books, or temples, or forms, are but secondary details.
In addition, he has also given the motto of the Ramakrishna Order as:
‘ātmano mokṣārthaṁ jagaddhitāya ca,’
‘One should work for the लिबेरतिओन् of oneself as also for the good of the world’.
These two together can be considered as the Philosophy of Vivekānanda. They are potentially capable of being expanded into full-fledged theories or even theses.
19. His Special Contribution
The special contribution of Vivekā-नन्द to the world in general and to India in particular may be listed as follows:
By creating the रमक्रिस्ह्न मथ् and the रमक्रिस्ह्न मिस्सिओन्, he not only rejuvenated but also recast Hindu मोनस्तिचिस्म् into a new mould, more relevant to the times.
He laid the foundation for and gave the right direction to the Indian independence movement, most of whose leaders were inspired by his speeches and writings.
He restored the national self-respect of the Indians by re-educating them in their past glory, advised them against blindly imitating the West, but also exhorted them to learn the best from it, in which we have been deficient.
He castigated the classes for their neglect, or even oppression, of the masses and inspired them to work for the latter’s upliftment.
He effectively pointed out that religion—in the sense of spiritual evolution—is the सोउल् of India and that all developments or reformations should be done only through that.
He laid great stress on material development of the country also, since religion is not to be imposed upon empty stomachs. It was his humanism and not मतेरिअलिस्म् that made him advocate this. He always felt that poverty and इग्नोरन्चे were dampers to spiritual progress and not its necessary conditions!
He disentangled Vedānta from its traditional Hindu setting and the stranglehold of the pundits, and, taught it as a universal religion applicable to the whole of mankind. In this sense he was a true teacher of the whole world.
Though he has generally followed शङ्कर’s Advaita in his discourses on हिन्दुइस्म् and Vedānta, he has made some original contributions too. The following points may specially be noted:
The वेदस् are not particular books but represent the eternal laws of the spiritual world, even as science represents the scientific laws of the material world.
The three systems of Vedānta—Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita—are not mutually conflicting. They give out the same Truth from different (and complementary) standpoints like the photographs of the same sun taken from different distances and angles.
The Supreme Being is Personal-Impersonal. The latter is not a negation but a fulfilment of the former.
Anthropomorphism cannot be avoided in any human conception of God.
He considers māyā as not a theory, but a statement of fact. What is important is to transcend it and realise that which is beyond it.
Thus he has made Vedānta practical, by stressing the sādhana aspects like non-attachment and yearning for the truth.
20. Epilogue
Perhaps, it is best to conclude with the well-known saying of another famous modern Indian leader who had the good fortune as a young man, of pulling the carriage in which Vivekānanda had been seated when he was received at Madras:
‘Swami Vivekananda saved हिन्दुइस्म् and saved India. But for him, we would have lost our religion and would not have gained our freedom. We therefore owe everything to Swami Vivekananda.’
C. Rajagopalachari (A.

vivāha
(‘taking [the girl] away in a special way;’ ‘marriage’)
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Vivāha or मर्रिअगे is one of the sixteen सṁस्कारस् or sacraments, but considered the most important of them all. Since even the Ṛgveda (10.85.6-47) contains a description of the मर्रिअगे of Sūryā (the daughter of the Sun-god) with सोम, most of the ṛks (mantras) of which are used even now in the traditional rites of मर्रिअगे, it can safely be presumed that it had become a well-established institution even by that time.
The main purpose of मर्रिअगे was to enable a man, by becoming a householder, to perform वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् and to continue the lineage by procreating worthy children.
Forms of Marriage
The smṛtis and the धर्मशास्त्रस् have enumerated eight forms of मर्रिअगे: brāhma, दैव, ārṣa, प्राजापत्य, āsura, गान्धर्व, rākṣasa and paiśāca (vide Manusmṛti 3.21; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.58-61).
In the brāhma form, the ड़थेर् of the girl gave her respectfully to a man of character and learning, after decking her with such ornaments as he could afford and without taking anything in return.
In the दैव, the decorated girl was given away by her ड़थेर् to a priest who officiated at a sacrifice commenced by him.
After receiving from the bridegroom a pair of kine, exclusively meant to be used in a sacrifice, if the ड़थेर् gave his daughter to him (who was considered worthy) it was ārṣa form of मर्रिअगे.
If the suitor pays money to the relations of the girl and also the girl herself, and accepts her as his bride out of free will, it is āsura form of मर्रिअगे.
If the bride and the groom choose each other out of love and passion, resulting in their union, it is the गान्धर्व form.
In the rākṣasa form of मर्रिअगे the girl is abducted or captured by force, by killing or injuring her relatives.
In the paiśāca form, the girl is ravished when she is sleeping or is unconscious.
The last two forms being of a criminal nature, are condemned. However, for क्षत्त्रिय heroes, the rākṣasa mode was permitted.
At present, it is only the brāhma form that is prevalent.
The system of fixing dowry and making it the main consideration in settling the मर्रिअगे does not seem to have existed in the ancient times.
Prohibited Relationships
The धर्मशास्त्रस् have prohibited मर्रिअगे if the boy and the girl belong to the same पिण्ड or गोत्र. The first prohibition means that the ancestor up to the fifth generation (of forefathers) should not be common to them on the मोथेर्’s side and the seventh generation on the ड़थेर्’s side. The second prohibition prescribes that they should not be from the same गोत्र or lineage (See GOTRA and PRAVARA.).
Though intercaste marriages were allowed in the ancient period, they were frowned upon during the later years. Similarly, remarriage of widows was prohibited.
Prerequisites
Since मर्रिअगे was considered a sacred and lifelong spiritual bond, several points had to be taken into account before finalising it.
First was the age. Adult marriages were common during the Vedic and the epic periods. Gradually the age was reduced to such an extent that child-marriages became the rule (vide वसिष्ठ Smṛti 15). However, the trend was reversed during the modern period (A.

onwards after the promulgation of The छिल्द्-मर्रिअगे Restraint Act)
The second consideration was the qualifications expected to be present in the bride and the groom.
The bride had to be a virgin, fairly beautiful, must have a sweet name and without any physical defects. A brotherless girl was not desired on religious considera-tions. The dharmaśāstra works do not mention anything about her educational qualification.
As regards the groom, he must have completed his ब्रह्मचर्य in the गुरुकुल and must be learned in the वेदस्. He must be a स्नातक (See SNĀTAKA for details.). He must be physically strong and virile.
Though virginity was insisted upon the bride, a similar condition was not laid on the groom since he could marry again if the first wife was dead or barren.
The स्मृति works were very particular about one point, viz., that both the bride and the groom must have come from a good vaṁśa or a pure family, blameless from the highest ethical standards.
Religious Ceremonies
The धर्मशास्त्रस्, especially the गृह्यसूत्रस्, have given long lists of the various rites connected with the sacrament of मर्रिअगे. They may now be described very briefly.
Vāgdāna
This is settling the मर्रिअगे through the oral promise by the ड़थेर् of the bride. Once it is made, it becomes binding.
Nāndīśrāddha
Also called Ābhyudayikaśrāddha (See ĀBHUYADAYIKAŚRĀDDHA.), it is an auspicious rite done in the morning to please the पितृस् or forefathers.
Madhuparka
This is offered to the bridegroom at the bride’s होउसे as a mark of honour. See MADHUPARKA for details.
Pratisarabandhana
This consists in tying an amulet on the bride’s hand for protection.
Parasparasamīkṣaṇa
First of all, a cloth screen is held between the bride and the groom. At the auspicious astrological moment, it is lowered and the couple see each other. The latter recites certain ṛks of the Ṛgveda (10.85).
Kanyādāna
This is an important rite wherein the ड़थेर् of the bride gifts her to the groom, asking him not to transgress her in धर्म (religious rites), अर्थ (worldly welfare) and काम (sexual desire). He has to respond saying ‘I shall not do so’ (‘nāticarāmi’).
Agnisthāpana
The main fire is established now for offering oblations with appropriate mantras.
Pāṇigrahaṇa
The bridegroom catches hold of the right hand of the bride with his own right hand uttering some Vedic mantras (vide Śāṅkhāyanagṛhyasūtras 1.13.2). This signifies his taking full responsibility of her.
Lājahoma
This consists in the bride offering lāja or parched paddy grains into the होम fire while the bridegroom repeats the concerned mantras. It is symbolical of fecundity and prosperity.
Agnipariṇayana
The couple go round the sacred होम fire and the ceremonially established water jar.
Aśmārohaṇa
Here, the bride is made to tread upon a mill-stone, to the north of the fire, with her right foot. It symbolises firmness of her relation with her husband.
Saptapadī
This is the most important part of the मर्रिअगे ceremonies, legally completing the मर्रिअगे and making it irrevoc-able. The couple take seven steps (= saptapada) together to the north of the fire. There are seven small heaps of rice. The bridegroom makes the bride step on each of the seven heaps with her right foot, beginning from the west. For each step she takes, the bridegroom recites some Vedic mantras (vide शाङ्खायन Gṛhyasūtras 1.14.6) praying for wealth, comforts, cattle, strength, and auspiciousness.
Sūryodīkṣaṇa
The bride is made to look at the sun to the accompaniment of the Ṛgvedic मन्त्र (7.66.16), desiring for the full span of life of a hundred years for the husband.
Hṛdayasparśa
The bridegroom touches the heart of the bride with a मन्त्र (vide Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtras (1.8.5) that signifies the union of their minds and hearts.
Gṛhapraveśa
The couple enter the होउसे of the bridegroom and then perform a होम.
Dhruvārundhatī-darśana
On the night of the मर्रिअगे, the bride is shown—and she is expected to see it—the pole-star (Dhruvanakṣatra) and the star अरुन्धती in the group of the Seven स्तर्स् (Saptarṣimaṇḍala or Ursa Major). This is suggestive of being firm in conjugal life.
Trirātravrata
The couple is expected to observe celibacy for three nights.
See CATURTHĪKARMA for details.
Maṅgalasūtrabandhana
After the सप्तपदी the bridegroom ties the मङ्गलसूत्र round the neck of the bride. She should wear it always as long as her husband is alive. See MAṄGALASŪTRA for details.
Airiṇīdāna
When the bride is about to leave her ड़थेर्’s place for her husband’s, a bamboo-basket, full of presents and a lighted lamp, is given to the मोथेर् of the bridegroom by the parents of the bride, with a request to treat her with love and consideration.
Epilogue
It is interesting to note that the main framework of rituals of मर्रिअगे and the Vedic mantras employed have practically remained unchanged over the last five thousand years.
The impact of modern एदुचतिओन् and contacts with other—especially the Western—cultures is bringing about vast changes in the Hindu society. Several amendments to the Hindu laws wrought by the Acts of the Parliament are also having their effects. Late marriages, divorces, remarriage of widows and intercaste marriages are not uncommon though still not very popular.
However, time and experience are showing—even upholding—that the basic values behind the Hindu मर्रिअगे system are sound and good. The Hindu society can ill-afford to ignore them.
